text: Do you know why a giant golden ball hangs inside one of the tallest buildings in the world? It weighs six hundred and sixty tonnes. As much as a hundred elephants.
This is Taipei one-oh-one. Five hundred and eight metres tall. When it opened in two thousand and four, it was the tallest building on Earth.
But Taiwan gets hit by typhoons and earthquakes. And tall towers are built to bend. In strong wind, the top sways back and forth, slowly, like a tree.
The tower is safe. But on the top floors, that slow sway can make people feel seasick. So the engineers hung a pendulum inside.
Between floors eighty-seven and ninety-two hangs a steel ball, five and a half metres wide. Forty-one thick steel plates, stacked like coins, hanging from eight steel cables.
Here's the trick. When the wind pushes the tower one way, the heavy ball lags behind. It swings the other way, and pulls the tower back.
It's tuned to swing at the same rhythm as the tower. Every push is answered by a pull, right on time.
Underneath, eight hydraulic pistons, like the shock absorbers in a car, turn that motion into heat. And the sway fades away.
It cuts the sway at the top by up to forty percent.
In twenty fifteen, Typhoon Soudelor hit Taipei. The ball swung a full metre, the most ever recorded. And the tower held.
And it isn't hidden. You can stand right next to it, and watch it move.
